newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iraqi oil delay supports Gulf refined products.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi oil delay supports Gulf refined products.

text.p: Delays in the start of Iraqi crude and oil product exports from its Mina al-Bakr Gulf terminal will support Gulf product prices and premiums into the fourth quarter, traders in the region said on Monday.
"The Kurdish situation put the (Iraqi oil) sale on complete hold...I can't see any sales, certainly products, till next year," one trader with a Western firm in the Gulf said.
Under United Nations resolution 986, Iraq is permitted to sell $2 billion of oil -- refined products and crude -- over six months in return for food and other humanitarian supplies.
But U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali delayed implementation of the deal after Iraqi forces attacked Kurdish rebels in northern Iraq on August 31.

Gulf traders had expected Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) to export gas oil (diesel) and fuel oil from the Mina al-Bakr terminal after initial crude sales, providing extra supply to meet anticipated higher winter products demand.

Firms in the region had entered product contract talks with SOMO and at least one had talks on securing product storage facilities at the port of Jebel Ali in Dubai in the United Arab Emirates, trading sources said.
"Jebel Ali was used regularly before the (1991 Gulf) war to store Iraqi products for shipment to Gulf, Asia and U.S. markets," a trader based in the UAE said.
Gulf product prices rose sharply earlier this month following U.S. missile attacks against Iraqi military targets in southern Iraq.
Gulf naphtha hit its highest level since October 1992 and gas oil since February this year on the missile attacks, a boom for oil product exporters Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Iran, Bahrain and the UAE.
Gas oil was assessed at around $25.90 a barrel fob Gulf on Monday, down from $26.15 on September 3, but way above the year-on-year comparison of $18.70.
Gulf gas oil premiums to independent price quotations stood at a healthy 80 cents, aided by tight middle distillate markets in northwest Europe, traders said.
"Gas oil is volatile but improving...Fuel oil is very strong," said a trader resident in the northern Gulf.
The rise in Gulf oil prices sparked by renewed tension in Iraq and winter stockbuilding has also improved refining margins in the region, with products outstripping crude gains, market sources said.
"Margins have improved somewhat...They are at their highest level for this time of year in two years...Refiners are making money, but nothing great," the resident trader said.
Fuel oil and gas oil marekts were strong, though there was some length in jet supplies, traders said.
